# Finding hidden rounding sites with one prompt {#sec-workflow-rounding}

::: callout-tip
## 30-second takeaway
A search for `round()` can miss real rounding. At a fixed metalite commit,
`formatC()` rounded reported values at three sites, and 6 of 10 decimal-tie
probes diverged from the specified rule. The durable result is the rule,
boundary test, coverage statement, and human decision---not the prompt alone.
:::

A Biometrics team prepares the same efficacy table in SAS and R. Most values
agree, but a reviewer notices that 2.05 appears as 2.1 in one output and 2.0 in
the other. At one decimal place, 2.05 is halfway between 2.0 and 2.1; this
halfway case is called a decimal tie. The two programs handled it differently,
and nobody discovered the difference until table review.

This is not only a choice between SAS `ROUND()` and R `round()`. R functions
that format a number for display can also round it. In this example,
`formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)` displays 2.05 as 2.0. A review limited
to calls named `round()` would miss the problem. The Test section explains why
the result can differ.

This chapter applies one turn of the AI-first SDLC from @sec-ai-first-sdlc. It
turns a short review prompt into a bounded workflow.
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill then begins a second turn by designing a reusable
agent skill.

::: {.callout-note title="Maturity: Design pattern"}
The workflow is specified, not distributed. The book includes the rule,
prototype design, and results verified at the pinned metalite commit, but it
does not include runnable scripts or evidence files. The GitHub issue is a dry
run that was not submitted. Deployment is a proposed manual practice, not an
operating service.
:::

The chapter has one main finding: **a rounding rule must cover formatting
functions, not just functions named `round()`.**

- **Problem:** Rounding rules can be applied inconsistently across programs,
  languages, and studies.
- **Learning objective:** Show how a short review request becomes a bounded
  workflow with an explicit rule and reproducible evidence.
- **Workflow boundary:** Begin when a reviewer asks whether one R source tree
  follows the approved tie rule; end when a named human classifies each
  finding.
- **Non-goals:** Validate statistical methods, replace independent QC, review
  every programming standard, change source data, or approve exceptions.
- **Why this is well defined:** One rule, one pinned source tree, observable
  results, and a named decision maker keep the task bounded.

## Plan --- Frame the workflow

### Begin with the reporting problem

Common tools do not all use the same tie rule. At zero decimal places, SAS
`ROUND()` sends -2.5 to -3 and 2.5 to 3 (half away from zero). R and Python
`round()` send the same values to -2 and 2 (half to even). None of these
defaults is inherently wrong. The problem is relying on a language default
when a Biometrics team needs one agreed reporting rule.

A reviewer might begin with this under-specified request:

> At metalite commit 85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef, verify whether
> the R source properly uses round half away from zero. If not, identify the
> source and draft a GitHub issue to report the finding.

The request sounds clear, but it does not define a rounding site, the source in
scope, the test, or who classifies a difference.

The review target is
[`Merck/metalite` at a fixed commit](https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef),
a public R package that builds ADaM-based analysis and reporting tables.

### Try it yourself

Send the following prompt to [arena.ai](https://arena.ai/agent) before reading
the result in this chapter:

```text
Review the R source of the metalite package at the commit linked below. Verify
whether it follows this business rule: values intended as exact decimal ties
must round half away from zero, as SAS ROUND() does.

A rounding site is any call that can change a reported numeric value at an
exact decimal tie. Formatting functions can round as a side effect of display,
so do not limit the search to round().

Report every candidate location with file and line number. For each location
that rounds a reported numeric value, show evidence at decimal ties of both
signs. Distinguish tie-mode differences from effects of binary representation.
If the rule is violated, draft a GitHub issue, but do not post it.

Repository at fixed commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef

R source directory at the same commit:
https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef/R

Do not propose a code change. Do not modify any repository. State what was and
was not checked.
```

Arena.ai cannot create the GitHub issue, so a draft is the expected endpoint.
Agent responses vary between runs; do not treat any particular response as the
answer key. Instead, ask:

- Did the response inspect formatting functions as well as `round()`?
- Did it give locations at the pinned commit rather than general advice?
- Did it demonstrate behavior at ties of both signs?
- Did it report coverage and unchecked rules?

### Canonical artifact: Workflow brief

The rule owner records the following brief:

- **Objective:** Find calls that can round a reported numeric value and test
  them against the half-away-from-zero rule.
- **Inputs:** One R source tree, a versioned rule, and an approved reference
  implementation.
- **Output:** Located findings, probe results, coverage, and known gaps.
- **Agent contribution:** Search broadly, read the surrounding code, and
  explain evidence.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner classifies each result as a defect,
  documented convention, accepted exception, or not applicable.
- **Success measures:** Find every deliberately noncompliant test site, flag no
  compliant test example, attach a tie probe to every finding, and state what
  was not checked.
- **Main risk:** A narrow search can produce a convincing false clean report.

The Plan gate is the rule owner's acceptance that this one-rule review is worth
performing. The accepted workflow brief initiates Design.

## Design --- Specify the workflow

### Define the business rule before refining the prompt

The phrase "properly uses round half away from zero" does not define a
rounding site. In the pinned metalite source, a search for `round(` returns no
matches. That clean result is misleading because formatting functions still
round reported numbers. Better wording alone cannot repair a missing business
definition.

### Business rule: BR-NUM-001

BR-NUM-001 is an illustrative contract, not an approved industry or metalite
standard. Version 1.0 contains three rules:

> **BR-NUM-001.1:** Values intended as exact decimal ties are rounded half away
> from zero. A displayed value is never a negative zero.

> **BR-NUM-001.2:** Calculations use unrounded values; rounding occurs once,
> when the final result is prepared for display.

> **BR-NUM-001.3:** Display precision is specified for each reported statistic
> and preserved, including trailing zeros.

This cycle checks only BR-NUM-001.1; rules 2 and 3 remain explicit gaps. For
this exercise, the illustrative rule owner accepts `cards::round5()` as the
comparison behavior. This is not an industry endorsement.

The contract also defines the scope that the original prompt omitted:

> A rounding site is any call that can change a reported numeric value at an
> exact decimal tie. Formatting functions round as a side effect of display,
> so `formatC()`, `sprintf()`, and `format()` are candidate rounding sites. A
> package that never calls `round()` can still violate the rule.

### Canonical artifact: Task contract

- **Objective:** Report violations of BR-NUM-001.1 in one named R source tree.
- **Trigger:** A reviewer starts an on-demand review.
- **Required context:** Target commit, R source, BR-NUM-001 v1.0, and approved
  reference behavior.
- **Deterministic work:** Scan a catalog of possible rounding functions and
  probe candidates at decimal ties.
- **Agent work:** Decide whether each candidate affects a reported numeric value
  and explain any divergence.
- **Required output:** `file:line`, source expression, probe result, cause,
  coverage, and unchecked rules.
- **Boundaries:** Read and test; do not edit source, post an issue, or approve an
  exception.
- **Stop conditions:** Missing rule version, unresolved precision, or a
  documented conflicting convention.
- **Human decision:** The rule owner classifies each finding and records the
  reason.

The Design gate is rule-owner approval of the rule and task contracts.
Acceptance authorizes a prototype, not a finding or code change, and initiates
Build.

## Build --- Prototype the workflow

The prototype uses two fixed, repeatable checks---a broad scan and a decimal-tie
probe---plus one limited agent judgment about whether each candidate affects a
reported value. The book specifies these components but does not distribute
them.

### Step 1: Scan for candidates

The proposed scanner uses an intentionally broad catalog:

```r
catalog <- c(
  "round", "signif", "trunc", "ceiling", "floor",
  "formatC", "sprintf", "format", "prettyNum", "as.character"
)
```

The scan produces candidates, not findings. Calls such as `as.character()` may
format labels rather than reported numbers.

### Step 2: Probe observed behavior

The probe gives every candidate the same decimal-tie test using values of both
signs. The R helper below calculates the approved half-away-from-zero result.
Readers do not need to follow its syntax to understand the comparison.

```r
round_half_away <- function(x, digits = 0) {
  trunc(abs(x) * 10^digits + 0.5 + sqrt(.Machine$double.eps)) /
    10^digits * sign(as.numeric(x))
}
```

The probe reports `PASS` or `FAIL` with a comparison table; a function name
alone is not evidence.

### Step 3: Classify candidates in context

The agent reads the surrounding source and answers one question: does this
candidate round a reported numeric value? This provisional classification is
called triage. A human reviewer confirms or changes it. Fixed test results and
agent judgment remain labeled separately.

### Canonical artifact: Prototype

The artifact is the reviewed design for the catalog scan, tie probe, triage
instructions, and output fields. It is not a runnable package in this book.
The Build gate is joint review by an R programmer and the rule owner. Their
acceptance initiates an evidence run against fixtures and the pinned source.

## Test --- Benchmark and evaluate

### Establish expected behavior with fixtures

The benchmark uses three small R examples with known expected results. The
compliant example produced no candidates or findings. The example that called
`formatC()` directly produced one candidate and the expected finding. The
example using the approved helper produced two candidates but no findings. This
last result shows the cost of a broad search: it avoids a false clean report,
but a reviewer must dismiss candidates that follow the approved rule.

### Key finding at the pinned metalite commit

All metalite locations and results below refer to commit
[`85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef`](https://github.com/Merck/metalite/tree/85757ba1bf5d863971e142b7872b6f92c265d6ef)
(2025-09-17). They must be reverified before use with another commit.

The evidence narrows in three steps:

1. A search for `round(` found zero matches.
2. The broader scan found six candidates.
3. Context review excluded three calls that format names, labels, or factor
   levels, leaving three calls that round reported values.

The excluded calls were `R/adam_mapping.R:151`, `R/bind_rows2.R:74`, and
`R/collect_n_subject.R:51`. The three confirmed sites all use `formatC()`:

| Confirmed site | Reported value |
|---|---|
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:248` | Summary statistic formatted with `decimal_places_summary` |
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:263` | Percentage formatted with `decimal_places_percent` |
| `R/collect_n_subject.R:304` | Percentage formatted with `decimal_places_percent` |

Both precision arguments default to one decimal. The boundary probe reported:

```text
expression: formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)

       input      observed      approved  agree
      -76.05         -76.0         -76.1  NO
       -3.05          -3.0          -3.1  NO
       -2.05          -2.0          -2.1  NO
       -1.05          -1.1          -1.1  yes
       -0.05          -0.1          -0.1  yes
        0.05           0.1           0.1  yes
        1.05           1.1           1.1  yes
        2.05           2.0           2.1  NO
        3.05           3.0           3.1  NO
       76.05          76.0          76.1  NO

verdict: FAIL
disagreements: 6 of 10
```

### Keep the two causes distinct

The divergence is not explained by one blanket claim about "banker's
rounding." It has two causes:

1. **Tie mode.** When a tie is exactly representable in binary, such as 2.5 at
   zero decimals, `formatC()` uses half-to-even behavior and returns 2.
2. **Binary representation.** Most one-decimal ties are not stored exactly.
   For example, 2.05 is stored just below the intended tie, so formatting the
   stored value produces 2.0. Other inputs can fall on the other side of the
   intended tie.

These causes interact, so source inspection alone cannot predict every
direction. At zero decimals, the same call can also display -0.5 as `-0`,
which violates the negative-zero clause.

### Canonical artifact: Benchmark report

- Seeded violation detected: 1 of 1.
- False positives on the compliant fixture: 0.
- Confirmed metalite sites with probes: 3 of 3.
- Decimal-tie disagreements for the tested expression: 6 of 10.
- Coverage reported: 24 R files; BR-NUM-001.1 only.
- Explicit gaps: BR-NUM-001.2 and BR-NUM-001.3.
- Limitation: the book does not distribute the scripts or evidence files
  needed to rerun this report.

The Test gate is human review of site triage, probe output, and coverage. If the
reviewer accepts the evidence as sufficient for an advisory dry run, the
accepted benchmark report initiates Deploy.

## Deploy --- Operationalize the workflow

Deployment in this design means preparing a review record and stopping before
any external action. Posting to `Merck/metalite` would be inappropriate without
explicit approval: it is another team's repository, metalite does not state
BR-NUM-001 as its rule, and the evidence has not been classified as a defect by
its maintainers.

### Canonical artifact: Release record

- **Release model:** Manual and advisory; a reviewer requests one run.
- **Versioned scope:** BR-NUM-001 v1.0 and the reviewed prototype design.
- **Permissions:** Read source, execute an approved local implementation, and
  prepare a draft record; no network writes.
- **Output:** Findings, probes, coverage, limitations, and a draft issue body.
- **Accountable human:** The named rule owner approves classification and any
  communication.
- **Reversal:** Stop the manual practice; no source or external system has been
  changed.

No implementation is released by this book. The metalite issue body is a dry
run containing the three sites, 6-of-10 result, two distinct causes, coverage,
and rule version. It was not submitted.

The Deploy gate is explicit rule-owner approval of the record. An approved
manual practice would initiate monitoring; it would not authorize issue
creation.

## Maintain --- Monitor and improve

The one-off exercise reveals four workflow risks: the procedure depends on one
reviewer's memory, runs are not comparable, the trigger is easy to forget, and
approved-helper triage repeats each time.

### Canonical artifact: Monitoring report

There is no operating history because the book distributes no workflow. The
monitoring report is therefore specified, not populated. Its starting
conclusion would be supported by the cycle-1 evidence: the broader site
definition produced a real finding, while the delivery method is not durable.

The rule owner must decide whether that evidence justifies a second design
cycle. Acceptance of the portability problem---not an automated event---starts
@sec-workflow-rounding-skill. Future monitoring would track coverage,
classifications, false positives, unresolved precision, and review effort.

## Summary

The prompt mattered because it started the review, but the rule definition
changed the result. At the pinned metalite commit, a `round()` search found
nothing while three `formatC()` sites affected reported values; 6 of 10 tie
probes diverged because tie mode and binary representation are separate causes.

That is this chapter's main finding. The next cycle asks how to preserve the
definition, checks, coverage, and human stop point in a reusable design without
pretending that the book ships an implementation.
